q: Explain why plasma without fibrinogen never clots.
Fibrinogen is the soluble protein that thrombin turns into insoluble fibrin. With no fibrinogen, no fibrin mesh can form.
Blood for transfusion is stored with citrate. Use the data to explain why.
Citrate removes calcium ions, which the clotting cascade needs, so stored blood does not clot; adding calcium back restores clotting (13 s).
Haemophilia plasma clots slowly, not never. Explain this, and the effect of factor VIII.

Only one factor is missing, so the cascade still runs slowly by other routes. Adding factor VIII restores a normal time, showing that factor VIII is the missing protein: it can be given as a treatment.
Explain why extra thrombin shortens the clotting time.
Thrombin is the enzyme that converts fibrinogen to fibrin: more enzyme, faster reaction.
Suggest why clotting is slower at 10 °C.
The cascade is a chain of enzyme reactions, which are slower at low temperature.

18.t: Working with data: HIV over ten years
q: Describe the change in helper T-cells in the first year.
A sharp fall to 550 (45% lower) at 3 months, then a partial recovery to 780 by 1 year.
Explain why the virus level falls between 3 months and 1 year.
The adaptive immune response: plasma cells make antibodies against HIV and cytotoxic T-cells kill infected cells.
AIDS is diagnosed when helper T-cells fall below 200 mm⁻³. Estimate when this patient reached it.
At about 8.5 to 9 years.
Explain the relationship between virus level and helper T-cell count after year 4.
HIV infects and destroys helper T-cells, so as the virus multiplies the count falls. With fewer helper T-cells, fewer B-cells are activated and antibodies fall, so the virus multiplies even faster.
Suggest why an antibody test can be negative in the first weeks after infection.
Antibodies take several weeks to be made, even though the virus level is already very high (the "window period").

27.t: Working with data: evaluating pandemic figures
q: Calculate the percentage change in cases in X from week 1 to week 3.
Calculate how much higher, as a percentage, X’s cases were than Y’s in week 3.
Explain how the difference in testing affects this comparison.
X tests six times as many people, so it finds more of its cases. Y probably misses many, so the real difference may be much smaller, or even reversed.
Suggest two other measures that would compare the countries more fairly.
Any two: deaths or excess deaths per 100 000; hospital admissions; the percentage of tests that are positive; random sample surveys.
Suggest two reasons, other than less testing, why X’s cases fell after week 3.
Any two: lockdown, masks or distancing; immunity from infection or vaccination; people changing behaviour; seasonal effects.
